There is a small room in my mind that looks like a station platform at two in the morning. The benches are empty, the lights are a little too bright and a little dusty; there is always that smell of metal and hot coffee, the smell someone who has been awake for too long might have on their jacket. Trains come and go in fragments—snatches of memory, overheard conversations, the glint of something you could not name at first. Sometimes I step onto one. Sometimes I sit and wait. The timetable is written in a language I can read but never quite understand.

Outside, the city goes about its slow, indifferent miracles. Neon and sodium lamps flicker like distant stars brought down to street level, and a taxi idling at an intersection looks like a beetle paused at the lip of the world. A woman with a scarf too bright for the season walks fast and sings to herself, or else hums the tune of a poem she cannot remember. Someone else leans on the corner of an old shop and counts the change of the day in his palm, eyes focused on not much at all. Even the pigeons have their routines—their own agendas, their own stubborn, tiny rebellions against the plans of people who think the city belongs to them.

I keep a list of unfinished sentences. They pile up like the tally marks on a tree trunk, notches carved by seasons I cannot name. There are sentences that start in the head with the easy urgency of clarity and end in the mouth like a question. There are sentences that feel like they will solve everything if only they could finish themselves. Usually they do not. They wait instead, patient as spiders, until some small thing brushes the web and the sentence closes in a ripple of meaning I remember for a week and then lose to a new weather system.

Possibility tastes like metal sometimes. Other times it tastes like bread. There is a particular kind of possibility that appears on a Wednesday afternoon, when the sun leans in through the blinds at an angle that spells out a word I cannot quite read. It feels like an invitation: take a different turn, send that message, jump on the bus, rearrange the shelf. The cost of possibility is also variable—rarely money, often a small, precise amount of courage. Courage is not dramatic, most of the time. It is making a call at the exact moment fear thinks you cannot. It is opening a door. It is saying the sentence you have been saving.

I remember once walking down a street where every storefront was a different story about longing. A florist that sold exclamation points instead of roses, a hardware store that fixed broken beginnings, a bakery that sold apologies wrapped in twine. I wanted everything. I bought a small bag of beginnings and carried them home like contraband. They were light in my hands and heavy in my pockets. At home, I spread them on the table and arranged them like seeds. Some of them sprouted into the everyday plants of habit—watered and rehomed and accepted. Others refused. They curled their edges and turned invisible. I kept watering them anyway, because hope is a plant that often thrives on ritual rather than chemistry.

There is an old radio in a thrift shop that plays only songs that could not be catalogued. It hums a frequency of nonsense and truth, a broadcast from some neighborhood of the world where words are currency and stories are the law. I press my ear to it sometimes, and I hear a conversation about whether a memory is more faithful than a lie. The radio insists they are the same thing, only dressed differently. Somewhere in the static, a child laughs—a sudden, crystalline note. The sound is simple and absolute and fills the room like rain.

People collect things to be near the edges of themselves they cannot visit directly. They collect maps, stamps, photographs, the shells of beetles, the first two chapters of novels they never finished. I collect the small acts of generosity from strangers—the man who hands his umbrella to a woman running across a flooded street, the teenager who pauses his music to help a lost tourist, the commuter who gives up a seat with no fanfare. They are pieces that fit into a pocketed vest of humanity, and I wear that vest when the weather is indefinite.

Words are a dangerous plumbing. Once you open them they run everywhere. Sometimes they flood entire neighborhoods of feeling. Other times they are the trickle in a pipe that tells you about the whole building if you listen carefully. Language is capable of creating a home or of demolishing an empire. I think of the lullabies that softened a century and the manifestos that hardened it beyond recognition. To speak is to be held accountable by the acoustics of history and the empathy of neighbors. Yet silence is not an exit; it is a landscape in which things grow without light and you must decide whether you will plant a candle or wait for the sun to invent itself again.

There is comfort in the small, measureable things: the exact way tea tastes when you have left it to cool for thirty-seven seconds; the geometry of a perfect shelf stacked by someone who respects rectangles; the timing of the last light before a storm where the whole city pauses as if inhaling. These are the tiny rituals I trust. They are anchors, not because they guarantee anything but because they are repeatable. Each repetition is a vote for a version of the world you prefer to live in. Votes accumulate. Sometimes they elect a life.

What comes to me comes as fragments and sometimes in orchestral sweeps. A scene arrives—two strangers on a bridge exchanging stories about the birds below, or an old woman teaching a child how to fold a paper crane—to be followed by reflections like footprints. I do not try to stitch them all into a single cloak. The world is too various for one size. Instead I make pockets: pockets for grief, pockets for joy, pockets for the things that are too fragile to be kept in the sunlight. Pockets are democratic. They ask nothing but to be opened and found.

Tonight, the platform is empty again. The lights still hum their soft, domestic electricity. Somewhere a kettle clicks off. In the distance, a train chooses a line and moves on. I am both passenger and station keeper, checking the timetable with a smile I cannot see. There are sentences waiting, and possibilities that taste of coffee grounds and sourdough. If you were to step onto this platform you would find a bench with room for two and a small thermos of tea that is exactly the right temperature. You would find that the timetable occasionally makes sense and that sometimes the train brings you exactly where you were going, and sometimes it takes you to a different city that becomes your favorite by the time you learn how to name its streets.
